title: A Gel That Could Regrow Tooth Enamel
hook: Enamel is the one part of a tooth your body can't rebuild once it's gone. A new fluoride-free gel aims to change that — coaxing saliva to grow a fresh mineral layer.
key_points: Enamel doesn't regenerate naturally, so damage from decay is normally permanent.
The experimental gel is fluoride-free and inspired by proteins that build enamel in infancy.
It fills microscopic cracks and pulls calcium and phosphate from saliva into a new mineral layer.
Researchers report the regrown layer closely matches healthy natural enamel.
content_html: Brush all you like — once tooth enamel is worn away, your body can't grow it back. That's what makes a newly reported gel intriguing: it aims to rebuild the one part of a tooth nature refuses to replace.
extra_html:
As ScienceDaily reports, researchers developed a fluoride-free gel inspired by the proteins that guide enamel formation in infancy. Applied to a damaged tooth, the gel fills in microscopic cracks and draws calcium and phosphate out of saliva, growing a fresh mineral layer that the team says closely resembles healthy natural enamel.

The appeal is that it works with the mouth's own chemistry rather than simply patching a surface, as fillings and standard fluoride treatments do. It's still early-stage research, not something at your dentist yet — but if it holds up, it points toward repairing decay rather than just drilling and filling it. For now, the reliable enamel protection remains the boring stuff: brushing, flossing, and cutting back on sugary, acidic drinks. This is general guidance, not a substitute for a dentist's advice.

related.title: Brushing and Flossing, Done Right
related.hook: Brushing twice a day sounds obvious — but for two minutes, with fluoride, and adding daily flossing, is where most people quietly fall short.

related.title: Why Oral Health Matters
related.hook: Your mouth isn't sealed off from the rest of you. Gum disease and untreated decay are linked to problems well beyond the teeth — and most of it is preventable.

related.title: What Sparkling Water Really Does to Your Teeth
related.hook: Fizzy water is acidic, so people worry about their enamel. But soda's dip in mouth acidity was the deepest and longest — sparkling water's was brief, and never past the damage threshold.

flashcards.prompt: Why would a gel that regrows enamel be such a big deal?
flashcards.back_html: Enamel is the one dental tissue the body can't replace on its own once it's lost, so decay damage is normally permanent. A gel that rebuilds it would restore what nothing else can.

flashcards.prompt: How does the experimental gel grow a new enamel layer?

choices.text: It draws calcium and phosphate from saliva into microscopic cracks
It uses a high dose of fluoride to harden the surface
It transplants living enamel-making cells into the tooth

flashcards.explanation_html: The gel is fluoride-free and modeled on the proteins that guide enamel formation in infancy. It fills tiny cracks and pulls calcium and phosphate out of saliva to grow a mineral layer that closely matches healthy enamel.
